Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Principal Appellant, and XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Minor Appellant, are citizens of Nigeria, and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Principal Appellant, and XXXX XXXX XXXX, the Minor Appellant, are citizens of Nigeria, and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.

The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to find them to be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellants ask that the matter be referred back to a different member of the Refugee Protection Division for re-determination.

In accordance with paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),1 the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD, and finds that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor are they persons in need of protection.
The appeal is dismissed.
The Principal Appellant alleges to fear persecution in Nigeria because she and her son (the Minor Appellant) are being subjected to cleansing rituals from her husband's family.
The Principal Appellant's husband's relatives accuse her of practicing witchcraft. The Minor Appellant is also accused of being a witch, since he is the Principal Appellant's child.

Their refugee claims were rejected by the RPD on August 24, 2018. The RPD found that the Appellants had a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Port Harcourt. The Appellants allege that the RPD's analysis contained a number of reviewable errors.
The RAD carefully considered the merits of the appeal in rendering its decision below.
According to the Federal Court of Appeal's ruling in Huruglica,2 the RAD will review decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent analysis of the evidence.
The RAD will defer to certain findings of the RPD where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing the oral evidence at the hearing.
The Appellants are not making an application under section 110(4) of the IRPA to admit new evidence. The Appellants are also not requesting an oral hearing from the RAD.

The Appellants raised a number of issues in their memorandum regarding how the RPD erred in its assessment of Port Harcourt as a viable IFA. The RAD will address each of the Appellants' arguments in its decision below. Whether the RPD breached natural justice by accepting that the Appellants were being pursued by the police but also concluding that their fear of the police was speculative
The RAD finds that the RPD did not breach any procedures of natural justice.

In their memorandum, the Appellants submit that the RPD erred in natural justice by accepting that the Appellants were being pursued by the police, but contradicting this finding by concluding that the Appellants' fear of the police was speculative.

The Appellants failed to specify how or why this alleged error in natural justice occurred. The Appellants did not cite any instance where the RPD denied them the right to be heard or the right to an unbiased decision-maker, or any compromise of procedural fairness. These are the principles that define natural justice and govern the procedurals followed by tribunals.

In contrast, simply finding that the RPD erred in its decision and disagreeing with its finding does not amount to a breach of natural justice, by definition. Therefore, the RAD disagrees with the Appellants and finds that there was no error. Whether the RPD made an error in accepting that the Appellants were being pursued by the police but also concluding that their fear of the police was speculative

The RAD also finds that the Appellants were not being pursued either by the entire Nigerian police force or by a few corrupt police officers. In its decision, the RPD makes a distinction between a few corrupt police officers and the entire Nigerian police force.3 The RAD finds that the RPD was correct to find that the Appellants' were neither pursued by the entire police force nor a few corrupt officers.

The Appellants spent a significant portion of their memorandum indicating that the RPD had accepted the allegations regarding their pursuit by the police. The Appellants submit that if the RPD accepted that the Appellants were wanted by the police, then it is an error that the RPD did not accept that the Appellants feared the police, and found this to be speculative.

It is unclear how the Appellants concluded that the RPD accepted their explanation that they were wanted by the police. In carefully reviewing the decision as well as the questions posed to the Principal Appellant at the oral hearing, the RAD finds that the RPD did not accept that the Appellants were being pursued by the police.4 Rather, the RPD disbelieved that the Principal Appellant's husband's family had the ability to influence the Nigerian police force to do its bidding. The RPD further disbelieved the Principal Appellant's explanation that a few police officers had likely been bribed to arrest her based on allegations of witchcraft.

In her testimony, the Principal Appellant testified that she would not be able to live safely in Nigeria because the police have the ability to locate her in any part of the country. However, no warrant had been issued for her arrest. The Principal Appellant was unable to explain how frequently the police came to look for her since she came to Canada in 2016.

The Principal Appellant was provided numerous opportunities during her hearing to explain whether she knew how her husband's family had the influence and the ability to convince the Nigerian police force that she and her son were practicing witchcraft. The RAD finds that the Principal Appellant was continually evasive during the RPD's questioning about her in-laws and their influence on the police force, and continued to provide details unrelated to the questions posed to her.5

The Appellants submit that the RPD accepted that corruption was rife in Nigeria in its decision.6 The Appellants explained that although there was no definite proof of bribery in the Appellants' case, it is more likely than not that the police were bribed when taking into account the evidence and testimony accepted by the RPD.7 The Appellants submit that their written and oral evidence are sufficient to demonstrate that the police were being bribed to locate them everywhere in the country, yet they provide no examples or references to any evidence in their memorandum.

The Principal Appellant indicated that she would not be safe in Port Harcourt because the police have been bribed to locate and arrest her.8 However, the standard of proof regarding whether an IFA is safe is made on a balance of probabilities. A balance of probabilities is defined as being more likely than not that an allegation is true. Therefore, it is insufficient to simply assert that corruption exists within the Nigerian police force, and that bribery is a possibility. If an allegation is possible, this does not make it probable.

The Principal Appellant was unable to provide any explanation in her oral or in her written evidence, regarding how she came to the conclusion that the police must have been bribed to search for her. Therefore, the RAD finds that this speculative response is insufficient to explain why she would be unsafe in Port Harcourt. Whether the RPD erred by finding that police communications are poor and therefore they would not be able to locate the Appellants in Port Harcourt

The RAD disagrees with the Appellants and finds that the RPD did not err by finding that the Nigerian police did not have sufficient technological means to locate the Appellants anywhere in the country.

The Appellants submit that the RPD erred by finding that the POLCOM initiative in Nigeria was to provide "EVERY" police formation with telephone lines.9 The Appellants submit that this initiative does not mean that there is not presently any form of communication within the Nigerian police. The Appellants further submit that the RPD's finding that there is not effective communication in the police force is based on speculation.10

After carefully reviewing the RPD's decision, the RAD is uncertain why the Appellants believe that the RPD erred by finding that the goal of the POLCOM initiative was "to provide EVERY police formation in the country with telephone lines". The RPD's decision cites this exact quote from the same source in the objective documentary evidence as the Appellants' initial counsel's post-hearing submissions.11

Furthermore, the RPD did not indicate in its decision that Nigerian police lacked any form of communication. Rather, the RPD found that the current existing communication network is poor.12 As well, the RAD disagrees that the RPD's finding was based on speculation. The current documentary evidence indicates that there is scarce information regarding the extent of communication between police offices across the country, and on the obligation of police officers to report persons who are suspected of having relocated.13 The same article indicates that the National Public Security Communication System (NPSCS) "has come next to nothing, with the system incomplete and effectively mothballed". The Nigerian Federal Government has not maintained this security system and did not have the proper funds for the system to function.14

The Appellants did not provide any objective documentary evidence to rebut the existing documentary evidence, which strongly indicates that the police information sharing system is indeed very poor. Therefore, given the objective evidence, the RAD agrees with the RPD, and finds that the current communications system in Nigeria would not provide the authorities or the Principal Appellant's in-laws with the ability to locate her in Port Harcourt. Whether the RPD erred by relying on the Jurisprudential Guideline (JG), and whether reliance on the JG amounts to a breach of natural justice

The RAD disagrees with the Appellants, and finds that the RPD did not err in its application of the JG on IFAs in Nigeria. The RAD further finds that there was no breach of natural justice in relying on the JG.

The Appellants submit that the decision cited in the JG refers to a case regarding female genital mutilation (FGM).15 However, the Appellants' case is distinguishable because the subject of their claims is witchcraft. The Appellants explained that FGM concerns non-state actors, whereas witchcraft allegations would put the Appellants at risk of criminal charges.

However, the purpose of a JG is to promote consistency, coherence, and fairness in the treatment of cases at the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada ("the Board").16 The Chairperson has the authority to issue guidelines to Board members, such as jurisprudential guidelines, to assist members in their duties.17

This particular JG is meant to provide members with guidance on how to analyze IFA in Nigeria, when the refugee claimant is alleging persecution from non-state actors.18 Although the claim types in the JG and in the Appellants' case are different, the RAD finds that the JG is still applicable because the profile of the Appellants is similar to that of the claimants in the JG. Like the claimant in the JG, the Principal Appellant is also an educated Christian female who is fluent in English and Yoruba.19 However unlike the claimant in the JG, the Principal Appellant would be relocating with a young child, the Minor Appellant.

The Appellants allege that the police would be able to locate them in Port Harcourt. However, for the reasons discussed above, the RAD does not find that the Appellants are being sought country-wide by the federal police force.

Also, the RAD finds that the RPD did not breach natural justice by choosing to rely on the JG. In their memorandum, the Appellants submit that reliance on the JG is an error in natural justice.20 However, the Appellants failed to elaborate on how the RPD breached natural justice through its application of the JG. The Appellants did not mention any potential bias on the part of the RPD, nor did the RAD identify any natural justice violations in its independent analysis.

The JG on IFA in Nigeria was issued after the hearing was concluded, and prior to the decision being written. The RPD provided counsel with the opportunity to make submissions on the impact of the JG on the claims.21 The decision was rendered after receiving these submissions, and so the RAD finds that the Appellants were provided a full opportunity to be heard. The RPD clearly indicated that IFA was a determinative issue at the hearing, and consequently, IFA was the determinative issue in the decision. In its decision, the RPD clearly outlined each of its concerns with the case, and then applied the JG to its analysis, and fully explained why the JG was applicable. Therefore, the RAD finds there was no breach of natural justice by the RPD. Whether the RPD erred by finding that the Appellants can live in Port Harcourt, given that Yoruba is not widely spoken in Port Harcourt
The RAD disagrees with the Appellants, and finds that the RPD did not err by finding that the Appellants could live in Port Harcourt, given that they are fluent in English and Yoruba.22

The Appellants submitted that Yoruba is not widely spoken in Port Harcourt, and it was the RPD's error to assume that this was the case.23 The Appellants explained that only bankers and businessmen speak English in Port Harcourt, and this would leave the Principal Appellant at a disadvantage with communication, as she does not speak the local dialect. The Appellants further submitted that the RPD made this assumption without relying on any reference to the objective documentary evidence.24

The RAD finds that the Appellants also did not make any reference to objective documentary evidence in its arguments regarding the extent of Yoruba and English being spoken in Port Harcourt. Therefore, it is unclear how the Appellants came to the conclusion that the English language was only used by businessmen and bankers there. It is also unclear whether the Appellants consequently believed that the English language was not used by any other locals in Port Harcourt, outside of the group of businessmen and bankers.

In analyzing the objective documentary evidence, there are approximately 500 different languages spoken in Nigeria, and English remains the official language of Nigeria.25 Therefore, in a major urban city like Port Harcourt with a population of 2.343 million,26 it is reasonable to believe that the English language would be widely spoken to the extent that the Appellants would be able to adequately communicate in that city. The objective documentary evidence is silent on whether English or Yoruba speakers in Port Harcourt would face any serious challenges in communication, which would make it unreasonable for them to live there. The Appellants did not provide any additional objective documents to indicate that English and Yoruba speakers cannot reside in Port Harcourt.

The RAD agrees with the RPD, that the Principal Appellant is fluent in English, given that she completed her Basis of Claim Form and all her refugee documents in English, despite having used a Yoruba interpreter at the hearing. Consequently, the RAD finds that it would not be unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Port Harcourt despite any language barriers that they allege, given the objective evidence. Appellants can relocate to Port Harcourt as it is both safe and reasonable
The RAD finds that the RPD did not err by finding that there is a viable IFA in Port Harcourt for the Appellants.

After conducting its independent analysis, the RAD finds that the Nigerian police are not motivated to locate and arrest the Appellants. The RAD finds that the Principal Appellant's in-laws do not have connections to the police that would enable them to locate the Appellants anywhere in the country. There is not a sophisticated information-sharing system amongst the Nigerian authorities that would put the Appellants' safety in jeopardy. Furthermore, the Principal Appellant is a Christian, college-educated person who is fluent in Yoruba and English. The RAD does not find that it would be unreasonable for the Principal Appellant with her personal profile, to relocate to Port Harcourt. The RAD finds that the Principal Appellant's profile is similar to that of the claimant described in the JG. Therefore, the RAD finds that the RPD correctly applied the JG in its decision. The Appellants did not dispute the RPD's findings on crime and kidnapping, or the availability of healthcare, and so those findings are upheld.

Therefore, the RAD finds that the RPD correctly applied the legal two-prong test for IFA, and finds that Port Harcourt is a viable IFA for the Appellants, given that it is both safe and reasonable, on a balance of probabilities.

Therefore, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination and dismisses the appeal according to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA. The RAD finds that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. (signed) "M. Lee" M.
